title: Elasticity, Anchoring & A/B Pricing Mastery
description: Apply advanced price optimization techniques including elasticity analysis, anchoring effects, and A/B test interpretation to real-world scenarios.

interactions.prompt: A SaaS company raised its Pro plan from $49 to $59 (+20%). Monthly subscriptions dropped from 2,000 to 1,700 (-15%). Revenue went from $98K to $100.3K. What's the key insight?

options.text: Demand is inelastic (elasticity = -0.75), so further increases likely profitable
Revenue barely changed, so the price increase was pointless
Losing 300 customers signals serious brand damage ahead
Elasticity is elastic (>1), meaning they should revert the price

interactions.prompt: Shopify-style e-commerce platform considering price optimization. You can run a Van Westendorp WTP survey across 5,000 merchants or deploy a live A/B price test to 10% of new signups for 4 weeks. Budget allows only one.

options.text: Run Van Westendorp—captures full WTP distribution without revenue risk
Run A/B test—revealed preference data beats stated preference every time
Run Van Westendorp first, then use results to design a targeted A/B test later
Skip both and use competitor benchmarking as a proxy for WTP

interactions.prompt: When a pricing page shows a $299/mo Enterprise plan next to a $99/mo Growth plan, the Enterprise tier is functioning as a price ____ that makes the Growth plan feel more affordable.

options.text: Anchor
Ceiling
Discriminator
Decoy

interactions.prompt: Stripe is launching a new fraud-prevention add-on. Rank these price optimization steps from first to last in the ideal sequence.

options.text: Run A/B pricing test with two price points on new signups
Conduct conjoint analysis to quantify WTP across segments
Analyze competitive pricing and cost structure for margin floors
Optimize packaging and anchoring based on A/B test results

interactions.prompt: HubSpot A/B tests two pricing pages. Page A: plans at $45, $90, $360. Page B: plans at $45, $180, $360. Page B shows 38% more $180 selections vs. Page A's $90 selections at only 22%. Total ARPU is 26% higher on Page B. What's happening?

options.text: Page B's middle tier benefits from asymmetric dominance (decoy effect)
The $360 anchor on Page B makes $180 feel like a compromise choice
Customers on Page B simply have higher willingness to pay
Page A's $90 tier is cannibalizing the higher plans

interactions.prompt: Your B2B analytics product has price elasticity of -0.4 in the SMB segment and -1.8 in Enterprise. You need to grow revenue 15% this quarter. Which move do you prioritize?

options.text: Raise SMB prices 10-15%—inelastic demand means revenue gains with minimal churn
Lower Enterprise prices 10% to drive volume in the elastic segment
Raise both segments proportionally to share the burden evenly
Bundle a new feature into Enterprise to justify a 20% price increase

interactions.prompt: A major competitor just launched a free tier that covers 60% of your SMB use cases. Your SMB elasticity has likely shifted dramatically. How do you adapt your pricing strategy?

options.text: Immediately match with a free tier to stop SMB churn
Hold SMB price but accelerate differentiated feature development for retention
Re-run WTP research on SMBs, then repackage tiers around features competitors lack
Abandon SMB pricing increase and shift all revenue targets to Enterprise

interactions.priorContext: Previously you planned to raise SMB prices 10-15% based on inelastic demand. Now a competitor's free tier has likely made SMB demand far more elastic, invalidating your original elasticity assumptions.

interactions.prompt: You're redesigning your pricing page to maximize ARPU using behavioral pricing principles. Rank these tactics by expected revenue impact from highest to lowest.

options.text: Add a high-price anchor tier that few will buy
Highlight the middle tier as 'Most Popular' with visual emphasis
Show annual pricing default with monthly as secondary option
End all prices in .99 instead of round numbers
